extracted.intended_audience: journalists, journalism students, and media scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the criteria and considerations journalists and news organizations use to choose and frame stories (e.g., moral/social disorder, leadership, whose order is valued, source/audience constraints). Useful for analyzing newsworthiness and editorial decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose framing / investigative reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposes are news items 'framed' to make the search for moral disorder explicit, forcing those identified as transgressors into the difficult position of defending their practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposes reaffirm the moral values on which they are based; refusal to be interviewed is reported and becomes a virtual admission of guilt. Television documentaries are the primary genre for exposes. Examples: 'Migrant' (exploitation of migrant workers); 'The Selling of the Pentagon' (public-relations practices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral disorder stories — implicit value judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Many moral disorder stories treat routine phenomena (violent or nonviolent crime, political acts like logrolling, patronage) as violations of altruistic democracy; the specific values violated are often not made explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants are identified as transgressors and react accordingly; the story frames ordinary practices as immoral even when values are implicit. Coverage signals wrongdoing even if the reporter does not declare the specific violated value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media presence produces performative moral behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporters or television camera crews arrive, people 'perform' morally and physically — denying or hiding behavior that could be judged as disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public and private agencies spruce up environments when reporters are expected; documented examples include suppression of prisoner beatings when cameras present, and Chinese authorities temporarily 'opening' society during TV filming. Implication: presence of media can reduce observable disorder and distort facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order in the news must specify 'what order' and 'whose order'
rubrics_metrics.description: Order is an important news value but is meaningless unless one specifies which type of order and whose conception of order is being valued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different groups judge order differently (e.g., affluent see slums as orderly if crime doesn't spill over; parents vs adolescents have different orders). Analysts should ask which group's order the story supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of disorder shapes news conception of order
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception of order varies with disorder type: natural-disaster news defines order as preservation of life and property; technological disasters are weighted by drama (plane crashes > tenement furnace deaths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsworthiness is influenced by the kind of disorder and conventional hierarchies among disaster types; editors privilege more dramatic or symbolically important incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social disorder is public-area disorder; location matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Social disorder is typically defined as disorder in public areas; events in prominent public spaces are more newsworthy than similar events in private or marginal spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A protest in front of city hall or a police station is news; the same event in front of a store may not be. Looting on Fifth Avenue drew more attention than larger looting in a ghetto the same day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target of action elevates newsworthiness (political target effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary criterion of worthiness is the target of the demonstration or disorder: actions that touch high political authority (especially the president) are much more newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social disorder becomes political disorder when it targets government or top officials; strikes or protests often gain national coverage only once they involve presidents or federal institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officials as potential threats to political order
rubrics_metrics.description: Public officials can be treated as potential threats to order when they act demagogically or in ways that may encourage citizens to question legitimacy, thus undermining political order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists report concern about officials who may stir passions or erode trust (examples: George Wallace, Lester Maddox, and concerns during the Nixon Administration). Coverage focuses on the effects of officials' behavior on public trust and order.

rubrics_metrics.name: News values social cohesion — mores violations are newsworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories about violations of mores (not merely laws) are newsworthy because they are interpreted as threats to social cohesion (e.g., youth rejecting Protestant work ethic, drug use as rejection of adult rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage emphasizes signs of social disintegration (rising divorce, falling marriage/fertility, cohabitation) more than ordinary family conflict, framing cultural change as a potential breakdown of order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between social disorder and moral disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Social disorder stories monitor citizens' respect for authority; moral disorder stories evaluate whether authority figures respect the rules of the citizenry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although both draw on similar underlying values, they differ in subject (ordinary citizens vs authority figures) and in the angle of evaluation (respect for authority vs authority's respect for citizen norms).

rubrics_metrics.name: News privileges the order of elites and powerful institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The news pays most attention to and upholds the actions of elite individuals and elite institutions — public officials, national corporations, prestigious professions, and 'quality' universities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News supports these sectors when they obey 'enduring values' and tends to ignore routine activities of less powerful groups unless they touch elites; focus is on individuals who hold power in societal strata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential monitoring — government held to harsher scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional obedience is monitored differentially; the news tends to be much harsher on government than on other sectors such as private enterprise or professions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the news defends institutional authority generally, it applies stricter scrutiny and criticism to public agencies and officials when assessing adherence to enduring values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic and assimilation bias in news coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The news reflects and privileges a white male social order, favors middle-aged and older over the young, and supports blacks and women who assimilate into the existing order rather than separatists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News selection demonstrates bias: most routine newsmakers are middle-aged/older; youth appear largely in delinquency or protest stories; efforts to include minorities/women are often framed assimilatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership as a central news value — qualities required
rubrics_metrics.description: The news values leaders as maintainers of order and assesses them by personal qualities: honesty, candor, vision, physical stamina, courage, brains, strength, and ability to control subordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A leader's moral failings or inefficiencies mark weak leadership; the news emphasizes personal traits and treats leaders as the principal agents shaping social processes (rather than roles produced by institutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: News can create or elevate leaders through selective coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists often single out one spokesperson in groups, thereby creating or making a leader by concentrating attention on that individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This manufacturing of leaders occurs for practical reasons (accessible spokespersons) and has the effect of privileging certain voices or organizations over others (example: journalists choosing one spokesperson for participatory-democracy groups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criteria for 'leaders' in Time's list (institutional and personal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Time's project selected 'future leaders' on the basis of personal qualities (honesty, candor, vision, stamina, courage, brains), demonstrated dedication ('the spark'), absence of scandal, and institutional touchstones: civic or social impact occupations (politicians, government officials, businesspeople, educators, lawyers, scientists, journalists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list intentionally excluded many occupations (e.g., artists) and skewed to nationalized institutions and prestigious universities (Ivy League presence), producing an occupational and class bias in defining leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on routine sources and practical/audience pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Who appears in the news (or in projects like Time's list) is heavily shaped by the pool of regular sources journalists consult, audience considerations, commercial concerns, and practical editorial aims (geographic/political balance, demographic representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters solicit recommendations from university presidents, industrialists, and other routine contacts; editors respond to corporate or audience feedback (e.g., adding business leaders), and try to pre-empt criticism by maximizing women/blacks in lists—even when source pools constrain choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paraideology and the news' reformist tilt
rubrics_metrics.description: The news embodies an aggregate, flexible set of values (a 'paraideology') that is neither doctrinaire nor wholly consistent; it tends toward reformist/Progressive values (altruistic democracy, responsible capitalism, meritocratic government, antipathy to bigness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paraideology blends liberal and conservative elements (e.g., respect for tradition and support for reform), shaping what is reported and how issues are judged. The news' ideological stance is thus often characterized as right-liberal or left-conservative but is best described as reformist.

rubrics_metrics.name: News measures elites against transcendent 'enduring values'
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the news pays attention to elites, it is not simply subservient; it measures powerful individuals and institutions against a set of enduring values assumed to transcend those elites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral disorder stories can compel elites to relinquish or conceal deficiencies; however, the values invoked are often set by reformers and elites themselves, leading to partial overlap between elite interests and the values used to critique them.

rubrics_metrics.name: The president singled out as ultimate protector of order
rubrics_metrics.description: The president is portrayed as the foremost leader and protector of national order, moral exemplar, and agent of national will; stories question delegation, vacations, illnesses, or deaths as indicators of weakened control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News coverage treats absence of apparent presidential control as a potential source of panic or security risk; reporting emphasizes the president's symbolic and practical role in maintaining order.
